'''George William Gray''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|CBE|FRS}} (4 September 1926 – 12 May 2013) was a Professor of Organic Chemistry at the [[University of Hull]] who was instrumental in developing the long-lasting materials which made [[liquid crystal display]]s possible. He created and systematically developed [[liquid crystal]] [[materials science]], and established a method of practical molecular design. Gray was recipient of the 1995 [[Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.inamori-f.or.jp/laureates/k11_a_george/prf_e.html |title=George William Gray - Biography |work=The 1995 Kyoto Prize - Advanced Technology |publisher=Inamori Foundation |access-date=2010-05-02 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100624141325/http://www.inamori-f.or.jp/laureates/k11_a_george/prf_e.html |archive-date=24 June 2010 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

==Education and career==
Born in [[Denny, Falkirk|Denny]], [[Scotland]],<ref name=guardian-20130521>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2013/may/21/george-gray |title=George Gray obituary |author=John Goodby and Peter Raynes |newspaper=The Guardian |date=21 May 2013 |access-date=11 November 2013}}</ref> Gray was educated at the [[University of Glasgow]] and while working as an assistant lecturer at the University College in Hull (then part of the [[University of London]]) obtained his PhD in 1953.<ref name=telegraph-20130606>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/10104394/Professor-George-Gray.html |title=Obitury: Professor George Gray |newspaper=Daily Telegraph |date=6 June 2013 |access-date=22 June 2013}}</ref>

He developed his academic career at the college, which became the [[University of Hull]] in 1954, from 1946 to 1990. He was appointed senior lecturer in 1960, Professor of Organic Chemistry in 1974, and GF Grant Professor of Chemistry in 1984.<ref name=telegraph-20130606/> He remained an Emeritus Professor at Hull.<ref name=gray-reminiscences>{{cite journal |title=Reminiscences from a life with liquid crystals |author=George W. Gray |journal=Liquid Crystals |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=5–14 |date=January 1998 |doi=10.1080/026782998207523 }}</ref>

In 1990 he joined the chemical company [[Merck KGaA|Merck]], then became an independent consultant in 1996.<ref name=telegraph-20130606/>

==Liquid crystals==
[[File:Cyanobiphenyl LCD clock, RRE, 1973.jpg|thumb|Demonstration digital clock using cyanobiphenyl liquid crystals made at the Royal Radar Establishment in 1973]]
In 1973, in conjunction with the [[Royal Radar Establishment]], Gray showed that [[4-Cyano-4'-pentylbiphenyl]] possessed a stable [[nematic]] phase at room temperature.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.null-hypothesis.co.uk/article/245 |title=George Gray: Liquid Perfection |publisher=Null Hypothesis |access-date=2010-05-02}}</ref> This compound and other long-lasting cyano-biphenyls made the [[twisted nematic field effect|twisted nematic]] display ([[Liquid crystal display|LCD]]) popular. Gray wrote the first English book on liquid crystals, ''"Molecular Structure and Properties of Liquid Crystals"'', published in 1962.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://liqcryst.chemie.uni-hamburg.de/lcionline/liqcryst/lchistory/topics/c13b12.html  |title=Applications of Liquid Crystals |publisher=Liquid Crystal Group, University of Hamburg |date=2001-05-28 |access-date=2010-05-02 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20010528144646/http://liqcryst.chemie.uni-hamburg.de/lcionline/liqcryst/lchistory/topics/c13b12.html |archive-date = 2001-05-28}}</ref>

Gray was recipient of the 1995 [[Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology]] and was made a [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in 1991. He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1983, and in 1987 was awarded the [[Leverhulme Medal of the Royal Society]]. In 1979 he was awarded the [[Rank Prize for Opto-electronics]] and in 1996 the [[SID Karl Ferdinand Braun Prize]]. The University of Hull was the first university to be awarded the [[Queen's Award for Technological Achievement]], in 1979, for the liquid crystal joint-development work.<ref name=gray-reminiscences/> Gray has been a Director of the International Liquid Crystal Society.  Members of the [[British Liquid Crystal Society]] honoured his achievements by establishing the George W. Gray Medal for contributions to liquid crystal research and technology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lci.kent.edu/events.html#Gray |title=Upcoming Events - George W. Gray |publisher=Liquid Crystal Institute, kent State University |date=1997-06-06 |access-date=2010-05-02 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719040040/http://www.lci.kent.edu/events.html |archive-date=2011-07-19 }}</ref>

In March 2013, the [[University of Hull]] celebrated the 40th anniversary of Gray's seminal paper being published on 22 March 1973.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www2.hull.ac.uk/newsandevents-1/newsarchive/2013newsarchive/march/inspiredinhull40yearsago.aspx |title=The screen you're reading this on was inspired in Hull 40 years ago... |publisher=University of Hull |date=20 March 2013 |access-date=14 May 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130530020620/http://www2.hull.ac.uk/newsandevents-1/newsarchive/2013newsarchive/march/inspiredinhull40yearsago.aspx |archive-date=30 May 2013 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

[[Hull Trains]] named their first [[British Rail Class 222]] 'Pioneer' [[High-speed rail|high-speed train]] ''Professor George Gray'' in recognition of his achievements in the modern history of [[Kingston upon Hull|Hull]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hulltrains.co.uk/our_trains.html  |title=New fleet named to celebrate modern "Pioneers" |publisher=Hull Trains |date=2007-04-17 |access-date=2010-05-02 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070417033622/http://www.hulltrains.co.uk/our_trains.html |archive-date = 2007-04-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yorklc.com/news.php?news=2 |title=George Gray honoured as a "Hull Pioneer" |author=Martin A. Bates |publisher=The Liquid Crystal & Advanced Materials Group, University of York |date=2005-07-01 |access-date=2010-05-02 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718142549/http://www.yorklc.com/news.php?news=2 |archive-date=2011-07-18 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1953 George Gray married Marjorie Canavan, who died two weeks before her husband. In later life they lived in Furzehill in [[Wimborne Minster]], [[Dorset]]. They had three daughters.<ref name=telegraph-20130606/>
